text:
Lee Seung-heon, also known as Heon Lee in the U.S., has chosen a path that many other Koreans would consider too risky to take. He dropped out of college to work full time at Philyron, a San Francisco-based maritime technology startup he co-founded in June this year.
“Korean students and their parents feel pressure when it comes to choosing a career over a college education. But in Silicon Valley, I’ve met plenty of young Americans who dropped out of prestigious universities to start their own businesses,” he told The Korea Times. “There is certainly a cultural difference between the two countries when it comes to college education. I concluded that starting my own business was the right decision and that spending three more years in college would be meaningless because schools don’t teach you how to start a business and keep it growing.”
Lee, 24, initially studied political science at Boston University. After completing his freshman year, he transferred to the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor before returning to Korea to fulfill his mandatory military service. Initially, he planned to return to school to study computer science and political science, but he changed his mind.
Lee saw enormous opportunities in two simultaneous booms: the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and the thriving U.S. shipbuilding industry. He decided to seize the opportunities created by these emerging trends.
In the U.S., particularly in the information technology industry, dropping out of college is not considered taboo. This may be partly because several tech billionaires left university to build their businesses. Bill Gates dropped out of Harvard University and co-founded Microsoft with Paul Allen. Steve Jobs dropped out of Reed College and co-founded Apple. Mark Zuckerberg, Michael Dell and Dustin Moskovitz are among other prominent college dropouts.
Unlike in Korea, Lee said, real world experience, particularly experience working at startups, is highly valued in Silicon Valley. He believes this culture has made Silicon Valley a hotbed for innovation and encouraged more young Americans to pursue their own entrepreneurial ventures.
Philyron develops AI-driven thermal and acoustic sensors that can be installed on ship hulls to provide operators with critical information about the condition and lifecycle of onboard devices and equipment, including when they need to be repaired or replaced. The technology makes vessel maintenance more predictable and helps operators manage their fleets more efficiently.
After San Francisco Bay Ferry became Philyron’s first customer, several other U.S. government agencies also adopted the startup’s sensors. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is among the company’s government partners.
“Like other Korean parents, my parents initially didn't approve of my decision to leave college. But they have changed their minds after seeing the progress my business has made. Now they encourage me to keep doing whatever I want,” he said.
In July, Philyron secured $500,000 in investment from Andreessen Horowitz, also known as a16z, one of the most powerful and prestigious Silicon Valley venture capital firms. Since then, Lee’s maritime startup has continued to expand its partnerships, primarily with U.S. government agencies.
“At Philyron, we are a small team of four, including myself. We aim to reach the $1 million revenue milestone next year,” he said. “Currently, most of our clients are U.S. government agencies. We’d like to sell our products to defense operators.”
Lee wears two hats at Philyron, keeping him busy. Like the company's other engineers, he works on software development. At the same time, he actively reaches out to potential clients to market the company's products.
He said his network of industry insiders had played an important role in helping him secure contracts with U.S. government agencies. Among those who have supported him is Kevin Humphreys, a vice president at Saronic Technologies.
“Mr. Humphreys saw opportunities in our startup and invested in it. Currently, we provide our sensors mainly to vessels, but they can also be used in other types of vehicles, such as trucks and aircraft. Mr. Humphreys recognized this potential,” he said.
As a co-founder, Lee said his ambition was relatively modest: to keep growing the business and build a sustainable company.
“All of our staff members are smart and talented. They are all students at Stanford, MIT and Berkeley, and they work part time,” he said. “I’d like to have them join us full time. To make that happen, I need to prove that this company is financially viable enough to convince them to put their college education on hold and work here full time.”
